papers.title: Evaluation of clinical utility in emulated clinical trials.
papers.one_line: Fills in the practical details of emulating a trial that compares an estimated optimal decision rule against the standard of care, proposes several estimators of clinical utility beyond the single one previously available, and shows the estimand is defined relative to a standard of care that drifts.
papers.what_was_done: Dynamic treatment regimes personalize decisions from historical data but need not beat current practice, so clinical utility compares the average outcome had the whole population been treated by a proposed regime against the outcome had it received the standard treatment assignment mechanism, such as physician choice. Trials for this are rarely run, and an emulated trial framework had been proposed with one simple estimator and no operational detail. This paper supplies the detail and adapts several estimators from the dynamic treatment regime literature, restricted to a single decision point. Simulations show minimal bias and nominal coverage at a sample size of 2,000. A rheumatoid arthritis example works through sample selection for determining who belongs in the eligible population for the standard of care, selection of time zero for the emulated trial, and comparison against current medical guidelines as well as against observed practice, which the source framework had not considered and which the example shows to be informative. Because the estimand is relative to the standard of care, it changes when practice changes or when the population changes, so the paper recommends recomputing rather than transporting it, and characterizing observed treatment patterns explicitly so later comparisons are possible.

future_research.gap: The framework covers a single decision point; extending it to multiple sequential decisions requires time-varying confounding, sequential exchangeability and positivity across treatment histories.
future_research.quote:
Multi stage regimes introduce
additional complexity, including the need to model time varying confounding, ensure
sequential exchangeability, and maintain positivity across treatment histories.

future_research.gap: Conditions under which clinical utility generalizes to a different target population have not been derived and would have to be adapted from the transportability literature.
future_research.quote:
Conditions that allow generalization to different target distributions may be possible to
derive by adapting methods from the transportability literature [21].

future_research.gap: Comparing sustained regimes against the standard of care is unresolved because observed later treatments need not match the natural course under earlier interventions.
future_research.quote:
Furthermore, comparing sustained regimes to the standard of care is complicated by
the fact that observed post-baseline treatments may not correspond to the natural
course under earlier interventions [23].

problems.evidence: The estimand is defined against a comparator that varies by population and drifts over time, so transporting it requires assumptions on the treatment assignment mechanism as well as on covariates. The paper does not derive those conditions; it recommends recomputing the quantity in each setting and recording the observed treatment patterns so that later comparisons are possible at all.
problems.quote:
As we have seen with the data example, if the SOC differs across populations or
evolves over time, the clinical utility may also differ as it is relative to the SOC.

problems.evidence: The work is deliberately confined to one decision point, and the barriers to the sequential case are named as time-varying confounding, sequential exchangeability and positivity across histories. Identification of a dynamic regime evaluated against practice over multiple decisions is left open, together with the further problem that observed post-baseline treatment is not the natural course under an earlier intervention.
problems.quote:
Our analysis focused on a single treatment decision for clarity and feasibility. Many
clinical contexts, however, involve multiple sequential decisions, and extending our
framework to such settings would be of great interest.

problems.evidence: Where one estimator existed the paper supplies several and characterizes their finite-sample behavior by simulation, which is what a defensible default would need. The simulations establish minimal bias and nominal coverage at a sample size of 2,000 under favorable conditions, and no rule is offered for selecting among the estimators outside those conditions.
problems.quote:
Notably, under favorable conditions with a substantial sample
size (n = 2000), the estimators exhibit minimal bias and nominal confidence interval
coverage levels.

problems.evidence: Two protocol components that are usually left implicit when a decision rule is evaluated, who belongs in the eligible population for the standard of care and where time zero falls, are worked out explicitly in the data example. They are demonstrated for one application rather than specified as a procedure.
problems.quote:
Finally, in the real data example we demonstrate how one can select a time zero for the emulated trial comparing
the estimated optimal decision rule to the SOC or enforced guidelines.

papers.title: Target trial emulation to replicate randomised clinical trials using registry data in multiple sclerosis.
papers.one_line: Replicates eight multiple sclerosis trials in 14,111 French registry patients, reaching concordance on relapse rate in seven of eight and on disability in all six, while radiological outcomes agree in three of five and one of four, and absolute event rates diverge from the trials throughout.
papers.what_was_done: Eight randomized trials comparing two active disease-modifying therapies were selected for drugs approved in France before 2021 and commonly used, and each was emulated in the Observatoire Francais de la Sclerose en Plaques registry covering 42 centres from 2003 to 2022. Eligibility replicated each trial's criteria at the time of therapy initiation, with an added calendar-year criterion ensuring both compared therapies were available. Time zero was the initiation date, assignment was by the therapy started, and follow-up ran to one or two years under an intention-to-treat setting. Relapse rate results were concordant with the trial in seven of eight emulations, disability progression in all six where reported. Radiological outcomes were harder: new or enlarged T2 lesions concordant in three of five, new gadolinium-enhanced T1 lesions in one of four, and one trial could not be estimated at all because only ten patients in the rituximab group had sufficient MRI assessments. Relative effects agreed while absolute event rates were generally higher in the emulations than in the trials. Discontinuation and switching diverged sharply from the trials in one emulation, roughly 50 percent against 15 percent in the interferon arm.

future_research.gap: Placebo-controlled trials were not attempted because defining time zero and assigning a strategy for untreated patients is harder, and the clone-censor-weight solution adds substantial complexity.
future_research.quote: First, we only replicated trials with active comparators, as placebo-controlled designs pose greater challenges in defining an appropriate time zero and assigning a treatment strategy for untreated patients.

future_research.gap: Which confounders must be adjusted for is specific to each question, intervention, outcome and data source, so the adequate set demonstrated here does not carry over.
future_research.quote: However, each study question may have specific confounders, depending on the intervention and outcome being evaluated, and also potentially the data source.

problems.evidence: The paper states plainly that a successful replication programme does not license the next emulation, and lists what reliability would still depend on: data source quality, causal reasoning behind confounder selection with residual confounding always possible, and decisions about estimand, protocol, adjustment method and model construction. Eight successful replications in one registry and one disease produce no transferable warrant.
problems.quote: Finally, validating TTE through the replication of RCTs is only one step towards the broader acceptance of real-world evidence in MS but does not guarantee that all observational studies using a TTE methodology will yield unbiased causal estimates.

problems.evidence: Concordance is declared on relative effects under two agreement criteria while absolute event rates differ substantially in both arms, so the same emulation passes on one estimand and fails on another. The paper also states that discordance need not mean the emulation is biased, since it may reflect limited transposability of the trial, which leaves the binary verdict undetermined in the cases where it matters.
problems.quote: Importantly, discordance between emulated trial and RCT results does not necessarily indicate bias in the emulated trial estimate.

problems.evidence: The outcomes that failed to replicate are the ones whose measurement depends on protocol: MRI timing, gadolinium injection, technical parameters, interpretation and lesion definition all differ between trials and practice and between one trial and another. The outcome variable is not the same object in the two settings, and the replication verdict absorbs that difference as discordance.
problems.quote: Variability in MRI technical parameters, interpretation and radiological outcome definitions can also exist not only between RCTs and real-world practice but also among various RCT protocols.

problems.evidence: Under an intention-to-treat setting with discontinuation and switching at roughly 50 percent in one emulated arm against 15 percent in the corresponding trial arm, the two analyses labelled the same way are estimating the effect of assignment under very different amounts of subsequent treatment change. The divergence is reported as a source of discrepancy rather than modelled.
problems.quote: As an example, for the OPERA trial, DMT discontinuations or switches were more frequent in the interferon group in our emulated trial (~50%) than in the RCT (~15%), and less frequent in the ocrelizumab group (~5% vs ~10%).

problems.evidence: A registry of 14,111 patients produced one emulation whose radiological effect could not be estimated because ten patients in the treated arm had sufficient MRI assessments. The paper generalizes this: adequate sample size is critical for covariate adjustment, and the settings where it failed are exactly the newer therapies and the outcomes requiring dense measurement.
problems.quote: For the RIFUND-MS trial, the treatment effect on radiological outcome could not be estimated in the emulated trial due to the very small number of patients with sufficient MRI assessments in the ‘rituximab’ group (n=10).

papers.title: Critical evaluation of real-world evidence of repurposable medicines in the Alzheimer's disease drug development pipeline using a target trial emulation.
papers.one_line: Emulates 121 trials across 54 FDA-approved drugs in MarketScan claims for Alzheimer's disease, with inverse probability weighting on more than 600 confounders and prespecified balance diagnostics, and abandons a per-protocol estimand because no single adherence rule fits heterogeneous drug regimens.
papers.what_was_done: Two base cohorts were built from MarketScan claims for 2011 to 2020, one of individuals with mild cognitive impairment and one of individuals aged 70 or older. Drugs represented in Alzheimer's trials were compared against same-class or active comparators with inverse-probability-weighted Cox models adjusting for more than 600 potential confounders, under prespecified diagnostics: trimming for common support, weighted standardized mean difference below 0.2, and weighted area under the curve near 0.50. Forty-nine emulations ran in the mild cognitive impairment cohort and 72 in the over-70 cohort, covering 54 drugs across 37 second-level ATC categories. Six of 38 drugs in the first cohort and 10 of 53 in the second were associated with lower Alzheimer's incidence against same-class comparators. Active comparator analyses associated bupropion, trazodone, venlafaxine and zolpidem with lower incidence in the mild cognitive impairment cohort, with liraglutide added in the over-70 cohort. Exposure was defined by first prescription under an intention-to-treat framework with no modeling of post-baseline adherence or duration. Some drugs could not be evaluated in one or both cohorts because covariate balance was inadequate, and diagnosis rested on clinical assessment without amyloid biomarkers.

future_research.gap: The findings are internal to one claims database and need replication in an independent electronic health record source.
future_research.quote: Finally, while we maximized internal validation within the database using both same‐class and active comparator designs and multiple effect measures, replication in independent EHR database will be an important future direction.

future_research.gap: The effect of taking a drug against not taking it could not be estimated at all, only comparisons between active drugs.
future_research.quote: Third, we were unable to estimate the effects of taking the drug versus not taking the drug, nor evaluate the severity of neuropsychiatric symptoms due to database constraints.

problems.evidence: A per-protocol estimand was dropped across 121 emulations for one reason: no adherence rule could be written that meant the same thing across drug regimens as different as an antidepressant, a hypnotic and an injectable GLP-1 analogue. Defining equivalence classes of treatment versions is precisely what blocked the analysis, and the resolution was to change the estimand to keep the comparisons scalable.
problems.quote: This estimand may differ from a per‐protocol effect, but a unified adherence rule was not feasible across heterogeneous drug regimens; the intention‐to‐treat approach enabled a consistent, scalable analysis across all comparisons.

problems.evidence: Three positivity and balance criteria were fixed in advance and enforced, and the enforcement had teeth: some drug and comparator pairs were declared not evaluable rather than reported with unstable weights, semaglutide among them. What the diagnostics do not do is identify which patient histories lack support, so a failure removes a whole comparison rather than naming the region.
problems.quote: Moreover, some drugs were not evaluable across both cohorts or specific comparator groups due to inadequate covariate balance.

problems.evidence: The outcome is a claims-recorded clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia with no biomarker confirmation, in a disease where diagnostic accuracy is known to be imperfect, and the exposure misses anything bought over the counter. Both variables enter the models as error-free indicators and the misclassification is left unquantified.
problems.quote: The diagnosis of AD in this study was based on clinical assessment and was not confirmed by amyloid‐related biomarkers.

problems.evidence: An earlier diagnosis date and a slower disease process produce the same observed outcome under this design, so the estimate cannot separate an effect on biology from an effect on when symptoms are recognized. Using the diagnosis itself as the outcome also stops the analysis at that point, leaving progression afterwards unobserved.
problems.quote: The methodology employed here cannot distinguish between slowing of disease progression and delay of onset of symptoms.

problems.evidence: The paper runs 121 emulations with a documented protocol and prespecified diagnostics, and then states that its findings are hypothesis-generating and do not replace fully powered trials. The rigor of the emulation does not translate into a claim about the evidence it produces, and no scale positions this output against a trial result.
problems.quote: These findings should, however, be interpreted as hypothesis‐generating and do not replace the need for fully powered and well‐designed RCTs.

papers.title: Advancing efficacy prediction for electronic health records based emulated trials in repurposing heart failure therapies.
papers.one_line: Builds emulated trials on 59,000 Mayo Clinic patients for 17 drugs repurposed in phase 3 heart failure trials, and drops time-varying confounder adjustment altogether because biomarker measurement timing in electronic health records is driven by clinical decisions and resource availability.
papers.what_was_done: To predict whether a repurposed drug will beat standard of care in a heart failure trial, drug-target predictions were combined with electronic health record emulated trials producing surrogate endpoints from prognostic markers. The drug-target model outperformed baselines on the BETA benchmark, and the combined framework was evaluated on 17 drugs drawn from 266 phase 3 heart failure trials using Mayo Clinic data on 59,000 patients. The endpoint was the probability of reaching a normal prognostic marker level during follow-up rather than a time to event, chosen because the recorded timing of a biomarker change reflects when testing happened rather than when the change occurred, so a logistic model replaced a Cox or pooled logistic model. Per-protocol emulation was prioritized with inverse probability weighting for adherence on baseline covariates only. Time-varying covariates were deliberately excluded: splitting follow-up into fixed intervals would generate substantial missingness requiring imputation, so the authors traded causal validity for data completeness. Adherence was defined from prescription and drug order records extending to the end of follow-up, with order frequency as a proxy for ongoing use, and the authors state this does not establish that patients took the medication.

future_research.gap: Choosing which variable interactions to stratify on is not straightforward, and a more principled method for identifying the confounding and interacting variables is needed for electronic health record data generation.
future_research.quote: Developing a more sophisticated method to comprehend these variables is crucial for the process of data generation from EHR.

problems.evidence: The visit and testing process is identified as the obstacle and then handled by removing the variables it affects. Time-varying confounder adjustment, which is what makes a per-protocol emulation identifiable, is dropped because the measurement schedule is driven by the patient's condition, physician decisions and resource availability, and the paper states the trade explicitly as sacrificing causal validity.
problems.quote: By excluding time-varying covariates, we reduced imputation bias and improved data completeness and precision but acknowledged a trade-off: sacrificing some causal validity by not adjusting for post-baseline time-varying confounders.

problems.evidence: The time scale was abandoned because recorded event times measure testing occasions rather than biological change, so a time-to-event estimand was replaced by a probability of ever reaching a normal marker within follow-up. That substitution changes what is estimated, and the informative measurement process that motivated it remains in the outcome definition.
problems.quote: However, in our study, the timing does not necessarily capture the exact point at which the biomarker status changes (e.g., from abnormal to normal).

problems.evidence: Adherence, the criterion that defines who stays in the per-protocol analysis, is constructed from prescription and drug order records with order frequency as a proxy, and the authors state this does not ensure the drug was taken. The strategy being emulated is therefore defined by a record pattern rather than by a treatment version anyone could specify clinically.
problems.quote: While this measure captures ongoing treatment activity, it does not ensure that patients consistently take their prescribed medications.

problems.evidence: The whole emulation runs on surrogate endpoints derived from prognostic markers standing in for the trial endpoints, and the evaluation target is reduced to the direction of the effect rather than its size. The surrogate relationship is not validated; it is the mechanism by which the emulation is made to produce a comparable quantity at all.
problems.quote: While our evaluation focuses on efficacy direction rather than both direction and magnitude, our ET implementation adheres to the same causal analysis framework to estimate the likelihood of achieving normal prognostic marker levels during follow-up with a repurposed drug.

problems.evidence: Emulations on their own were found insufficient for predicting even the direction of a trial result, and the fix is to add biological drug-target prediction and stratification on variable interactions. That is an admission that the emulation is not calibrated to the trial it is meant to anticipate, with the gap closed by information from outside the causal framework.
problems.quote: By evaluating 17 drugs repurposed for phase 3 HF RCTs, we highlighted the inherent limitations of trial simulations for efficacy direction prediction based solely on EHR data.

papers.title: The GRACE Checklist: A Validated Assessment Tool for High Quality Observational Studies of Comparative Effectiveness.
papers.one_line: Validates an 11-item quality checklist against expert judgment, citation count and journal impact factor, reaching 71 percent sensitivity and 81 percent specificity, and states that no accepted gold standard for article quality exists to validate against.
papers.what_was_done: Twenty-eight observational comparative effectiveness articles published from 2001 to 2010 were assessed with the GRACE Checklist by 22 volunteers from academia, industry and government, producing 56 assessments. Ten senior experts rated overall article quality for decision support, and each article was also scored by annual citations and by the impact factor of its journal. Classification and regression tree analysis built four decision trees against expert assessment, citation frequency, impact factor and a composite of all three. The best predictors of quality were concurrent comparators, restriction to new initiators, equivalent outcome measurement across groups, collecting data on most or all known confounders and effect modifiers, accounting for immortal time bias in the analysis, and sensitivity analyses testing dependence on assumptions. Only sensitivity analyses appeared in all four trees. Against the composite outcome the checklist reached sensitivity 71.43 percent and specificity 80.95 percent. The limitations section states there is no accepted gold standard for article quality, that expert agreement was 52 percent among articles receiving multiple expert assessments, and that the checklist qualifies methodologic rigor but not applicability to a particular decision.

future_research.gap: There is no accepted gold standard for observational study quality against which any assessment instrument can be validated.
future_research.quote:
There is no single accepted “gold standard” for article quality
against which assessments such as the GRACE Checklist or
other instruments may be validated.

future_research.gap: Whether a study is applicable to the decision at hand is outside what the checklist can assess, and no instrument covers it.
future_research.quote:
Finally, the GRACE Checklist can only be
used to qualify methodologic rigor, not applicability to a given
decision.

problems.evidence: This is the closest thing the field has to a threshold: a screening instrument with measured sensitivity and specificity against external criteria, distinguished from the surrounding guidance documents by having been validated at all. The comparison table lists eight guidance documents developed by consensus alone. What the instrument screens for is publication-level quality, not whether an estimate is adequate for a specific regulatory decision, which the paper states it cannot assess.
problems.quote:
Although many guidance documents have been developed for
the evaluation of observational study quality, only the GRACE
Checklist has been validated against external measures of quality.
problems.locator: What is already known about this subject

problems.evidence: Two of the three external criteria against which the instrument was validated are citation count and journal impact factor, which measure attention rather than correctness, and the third, expert judgment, agreed with itself only 52 percent of the time. An instrument calibrated to these criteria carries no argument that it transfers to a question the validation set did not contain.
problems.quote:
One of the most intuitively
appealing measures, an overall assessment of quality by recognized experts in the design and conduct of observational studies, showed relatively low agreement (52%) between the reviewers for the articles that received multiple expert assessments.12

problems.evidence: The checklist item that predicted quality in all four trees is whether the study reported sensitivity analyses showing how much the estimate depended on its assumptions, which is a partial assumption dashboard: it records that dependence was examined without distinguishing assumptions that can be diagnosed from those that cannot.
problems.quote: Only sensitivity analyses appeared consistently as a predictor of quality in all 4 trees.

papers.title: Statins and Risk of Lower Limb Revision Surgery: The Influence of Differences in Study Design Using Electronic Health Records From the United Kingdom and Denmark.
papers.one_line: Runs four designs on 189,286 joint replacement patients in two national databases and shows exposure classification moves the incidence rate ratio from 0.90 to 0.36 while confounder-handling technique and data source move it hardly at all.
papers.what_was_done: Patients with a primary total hip or knee replacement in Denmark and the United Kingdom between 1987 and 2012, 189,286 in all, were analyzed for the association between postoperative statin use and revision surgery under four designs: a case-control design matching each revision to four controls, a time-dependent cohort treating statin use as time-varying, an immortal time cohort misclassifying the postoperative period before statin use, and a time-exclusion cohort dropping that period. The time-dependent cohort gave an adjusted incidence rate ratio of 0.90 with 95 percent interval 0.85 to 0.96, close to the case-control result of 0.87 with interval 0.81 to 0.93. Misclassifying immortal time gave 0.36 with interval 0.34 to 0.38, and excluding it gave 0.65 with interval 0.63 to 0.68, because misclassification lengthens user person-time and shortens nonuser person-time while exclusion shortens nonuser person-time only. Risk did not fall with longer statin use, so the paper concludes there is probably no causal relationship. Confounder-handling technique, including several propensity score methods, and choice of database made no material difference, though absolute revision rates differed between countries. The magnitude of immortal time bias grew with more intense modeling.

future_research.gap: Whether the confounder data in electronic health records are good enough for the adjustment techniques applied to them has not been examined systematically.
future_research.quote: The confounding data in electronic health records are often limited by the quality of the data itself, but this has not been studied comprehensively before.

problems.evidence: One design decision moves the estimate by a factor of two and a half while every other decision in the analysis is inert. The paper's own framing is that the choice takes the result from biologically plausible to implausible, so the design parameter rather than the data determines whether a protective effect is reported.
problems.quote: The simple choice of how to classify exposure can substantially change results from biologically plausible to implausible.

problems.evidence: Propensity adjustment, propensity matching and conventional regression were compared and produced the same rate ratios, so the estimator debate consumed effort on a decision that did not matter while the decision that did was made by convention. Worse, the paper reports that more intense modeling amplified the immortal time bias rather than reducing it.
problems.quote: Interestingly, the magnitude of immortal time bias became larger with more intense modeling.

problems.evidence: Running the same protocol on two national databases with different structures is a data-fitness check performed rather than described, and it returned a negative result: rate ratios agreed although absolute revision rates did not, which the paper attributes to underrecording in general practice records. The check is post hoc and would not have stopped the study.
problems.quote: The use of different data sources was not a discriminating factor in this example of statins and implant revision.

problems.evidence: Implant failure is measured by revision surgery, which is conditional on the patient being fit for another operation, so the outcome variable encodes a selection the analysis does not model. The paper names this as a major limitation and then argues the resulting misclassification is nondifferential without evidence.
problems.quote: A major limitation of our study is that we used a proxy measure for implant failure—revision surgery.

papers.title: Response to letter, 'immortal time bias in retrospective analysis'.
papers.one_line: Reanalyzes the myeloma data with humoral response as a time-dependent covariate as requested, obtains hazard ratios of 0.59 for progression-free and 0.55 for overall survival, and reports the correction as confirming the original conclusions without showing the original estimate beside it.
papers.what_was_done: Responding to a letter identifying immortal time in a comparison of outcomes by humoral response, the authors note that the response rate was 79 percent among patients with progression-free survival of at least three years against 54 percent among others, with a p-value of 0.006, but that median time to humoral response was one month in both groups. They then reran progression-free and overall survival with humoral response as a time-dependent covariate. Comparing responders with nonresponders gave a hazard ratio of 0.59 with 95 percent interval 0.43 to 0.82 and p-value 0.0016 for progression-free survival, and 0.55 with interval 0.40 to 0.76 and p-value 0.0003 for overall survival, described as a 41 percent reduction in the risk of progression or death and a 45 percent reduction in death. The conclusion is that the time-dependent analysis confirms humoral response as a significant predictor of long-term benefit, in agreement with the original paper. The corrected numbers are reported on their own; the original uncorrected estimates are not restated for comparison, and the analysis remains a prognostic comparison of responders with nonresponders rather than a comparison of treatment strategies.

problems.evidence: The requested correction was performed and published, which is the correction loop working end to end on a specific paper. The correction is a time-dependent covariate, which removes the guaranteed survival but leaves the comparison a prognostic one between response groups, so it addresses the time-related bias without making the contrast a treatment strategy contrast.
problems.quote: To address the concerns of Hsieh et al. , 1 we reanalyzed PFS and OS using humoral response as a time-dependent covariate, as suggested.

problems.evidence: The reply gives the corrected hazard ratios and states agreement with the original conclusions, without reporting what the uncorrected estimates were. A reader cannot tell how much of the original effect was immortal time, which is the quantity the exchange was about, so the published record shows that the objection was answered but not by how much the answer moved.
problems.quote: This time-dependent analysis confirms that humoral response significantly predicts the long-term benefit of lenalidomide and dexamethasone therapy for patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, in agreement with the original conclusions of the paper.

papers.title: Validation of methods to control for immortal time bias in a pharmacoepidemiologic analysis of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors in type 2 diabetes.
papers.one_line: Benchmarks four immortal-time corrections against a randomized-trial meta-analysis hazard ratio of 0.92 in 3,928 Hong Kong diabetes registry patients and finds that the standard time-dependent Cox correction inflates the estimate far above the trial interval by worsening confounding by indication.
papers.what_was_done: Among 3,928 patients with type 2 diabetes in the Hong Kong Diabetes Registry followed to 2005, 284 developed cardiovascular disease over a median 5.45 years and 1,519 started renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, with 39.1 percent of user follow-up being immortal time. Because these drugs are established as cardioprotective, a meta-analysis of randomized trials supplied a benchmark hazard ratio of 0.92 against which each analytic method could be judged. Time-dependent drug-exposure Cox models and time-fixed models that moved immortal time from users to nonusers both produced hazard ratios above the upper limit of the trial interval, implying the drugs increase cardiovascular risk. Time-fixed models that included immortal time in the exposed period deflated the estimate. Only excluding immortal time without reassigning it to nonusers, which is contrary to the standard recommendation, produced 0.89 with interval 0.68 to 1.17, inside the trial range. Re-estimating the risk profile at the time of drug commencement did not remove the bias. The paper attributes the failure of the time-dependent model to the non-random risk profile of patients who start the drug, and notes the recommended reassignment itself attenuated the early hazard among nonusers.

future_research.gap: Whether the ranking of these correction methods holds for drugs other than renin-angiotensin system inhibitors is unestablished.
future_research.quote: Third, this analysis attempted to validate methods for addressing the effects of RAS inhibitors in T2D; applicability to other drugs remains to be confirmed.

future_research.gap: The findings come from one cohort and need confirmation in similarly designed studies.
future_research.quote: Last, the present findings were obtained from a single cohort of patients with T2D and need to be confirmed in other similarly designed studies.

problems.evidence: The estimator recommended in the methodological literature performed worst here, and the paper identifies the reason: correcting time-related bias amplified confounding by indication, because patients who start a drug have a particular risk profile that time-dependent models assume away. No procedure decides in advance which of the two biases dominates, so the choice of correction is itself an uncontrolled analytic degree of freedom.
problems.quote: In addition, a method used to control one source of bias might exaggerate bias from other sources, eg, the time-dependent Cox model worsened confounding by indications for RAS inhibitor use.

problems.evidence: The whole design rests on treating a randomized-trial meta-analysis estimate as the truth for one drug class and one outcome, and the paper states both limits of that move: the trial estimate may not apply in practice, and the method ranking may not transfer to other drugs. A method validated this way is validated for the benchmark, and nothing extends the verdict.
problems.quote: First, the effect size of use of RAS inhibitors on CVD was based on a meta-analysis of RCTs, 8 which might not be applicable in real practice.

problems.evidence: Immortal time and confounding by indication are violated together here, and every method examined addresses one while worsening the other. The authors state they cannot rule out that the method producing the right answer did so by two errors cancelling, which is precisely what a one-assumption-at-a-time sensitivity analysis cannot detect.
problems.quote: Whether the observed effects of RAS inhibitors on CVD, as determined by different methods, represent true effects depends on how well these approaches simultaneously remove the mixture of confounding effects of drug use indications and immortal time, and on bias from other sources.

problems.evidence: Thirty-nine percent of user follow-up in this cohort is immortal time, and the four ways of handling that interval, include it, exclude it, reassign it, or model exposure as time-varying, give four different answers spanning the null in both directions. The interval itself is a consequence of where follow-up starts relative to the prescription date, which nothing in the design fixes.
problems.quote: During a median follow-up period of 5.45 years, 7.23% ( n = 284) patients developed CVD and 38.7% ( n = 1519) were started on RAS inhibitors, with 39.1% of immortal time among the users.

papers.title: Immortal time bias in retrospective analysis: comment on 'Efficacy and safety of long-term treatment with lenalidomide and dexamethasone in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma'.
papers.one_line: Letter identifying immortal time in a published myeloma analysis that compared survival by humoral response, where response required at least six 28-day cycles so the responder group could not die in the first five months.
papers.what_was_done: A published analysis compared outcomes between patients with and without a humoral response to lenalidomide and dexamethasone in relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Because a humoral response was defined as requiring at least six cycles of 28 days each, a patient classified as a responder had to survive roughly five months, and no death could occur in the responder group during that interval. The letter states the general definition, that immortal time is an interval of follow-up during which the outcome cannot occur because of how exposure is defined, and applies it to this case. It accepts that humoral improvement may genuinely predict outcome in multiple myeloma, and asks for the analysis to be redone with response as a time-dependent covariate in a Cox model rather than as a baseline group label, then requests that the reanalysis be published.

future_research.gap: The original data have not been reanalyzed with response as a time-dependent covariate.
future_research.quote: We look forward to see such reanalysis of the original data.

problems.evidence: The immortal interval here is set by the protocol definition of response, six cycles of 28 days, so the amount of guaranteed survival is a consequence of a clinical classification rule rather than of any analytic choice. Nothing in the design process flags that a response definition requiring a minimum exposure duration creates a survival requirement.
problems.quote: ‘Immortal time' refers to a time interval during the follow-up period in which the outcome could never occur because of exposure definition.

problems.evidence: Humoral response is treated in the original analysis as a binary group label attached to the patient, when it is a status measured at a specific time by a specific assay schedule. The correction requested, making it time-dependent, is an acknowledgment that the timing of measurement is part of the variable and cannot be dropped.
problems.quote: In conventional survival analysis, the immortal time bias can confer a spurious survival advantage to the responder group if the response is measured in the middle of the follow-up period but not at the beginning of the trial.

papers.title: Randomized Trials Built on Sand: Examples from COPD, Hormone Therapy, and Cancer.
papers.one_line: Traces three cases where observational studies reported large benefits for a repurposed drug, two of which were later refuted by large randomized trials, and supplies a six-question checklist for detecting immortal time bias during peer review.
papers.what_was_done: Three episodes are set side by side. Hormone replacement therapy, indicated for menopausal symptoms, was reported through the 1980s and 1990s to reduce coronary heart disease incidence, a claim refuted by the Women's Health Initiative in 2002. Inhaled corticosteroids, indicated for asthma and used in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease without evidence, were reported to reduce all-cause mortality, a claim not corroborated by the TORCH trial. Metformin is currently reported to reduce cancer incidence and mortality, and those reports have already launched large randomized trials. In each case the spectacular effect is shown to be a product of time-related bias, chiefly immortal time bias, which disappears under proper analysis. The paper notes that promising observational findings pull animal and mechanistic studies behind them, which adds momentum to a new indication before anyone has assessed the observational methods. It closes with a peer-review box: if a cohort study reports a relative risk below 0.70, immortal time bias should be considered, and six questions flag it, covering whether treatment status was determined during follow-up, whether follow-up started at different times in the two groups, whether groups were formed hierarchically, whether subjects were excluded for treatment started during follow-up, whether data were reported on patients rather than person-time, and whether a time-fixed analysis was used.

future_research.gap: Time-related biases are established in pharmacoepidemiology but have not reached the subspecialty fields where the affected studies are published.
future_research.quote: While these biases are well-known in pharmacoepidemiology and have been described extensively in different therapeutic areas, 31 , 34 , 35 , 63 , 64 they do not seem to have yet sufficiently penetrated different subspecialty fields such as diabetes, cancer, pulmonary medicine, etc.

problems.evidence: This is a working detection instrument rather than a principle: an effect-size trigger at relative risk below 0.70 and six yes-or-no design questions any reviewer can answer from a methods section. It detects one bias and says nothing about the assumptions that cannot be read off a design description, so it is a screen and not a dashboard.
problems.quote: If a cohort study reports extreme beneficial effects (relative risks < 0.70) for a treatment, reviewer should consider immortal time bias as an alternative explanation and answers in the affirmative to any of the following questions should raise red flags:

problems.evidence: Two of the three cases were settled by a large randomized trial contradicting the observational literature, and the paper's reading is that the observational studies were flawed rather than that the populations differed. No procedure separates those two explanations at the time of the discordance, which is why the third case, metformin, is still open and has trials running on it.
problems.quote: Certainly, methodologically inaccurate studies, even if their biased results are replicated in different settings and by different authors, should not be the driving force in conducting randomized trials.

problems.evidence: The decision the paper is arguing about is whether to commit to a large randomized trial on the strength of observational evidence, and it offers a judgment rather than a threshold. Mechanistic and animal work accumulating behind a biased observational finding is described as adding momentum, with no point at which the accumulating evidence is required to be re-examined.
problems.quote: However, it is imperative first to carry out critical assessments of the observational study methods

papers.title: Metformin and the risk of cancer: time-related biases in observational studies.
papers.one_line: Identifies immortal time bias in 13 observational studies of metformin and cancer and time-window bias in nine more, showing that risk reductions of 20 to 94 percent are compatible with the biases and that the three studies avoiding them found no effect.
papers.what_was_done: Three time-related biases are defined and traced through the metformin and cancer literature. Immortal time bias comes from time-fixed cohort analyses that misclassify unexposed time as exposed. Time-window bias comes from differential exposure opportunity windows between subjects. Time-lag bias comes from comparing a first-line treatment such as metformin with second- or third-line treatments given at a later disease stage. Thirteen studies were found to suffer immortal time bias and nine not to have considered time-window bias, with others ignoring the time-lag issue. The reported reductions in cancer risk across these studies range from a relative risk of 0.80 to 0.06, that is 20 to 94 percent. Two studies recognized immortal time bias but used an analysis that did not address it. Three studies using the time-dependent techniques needed to avoid both immortal time and time-window bias found no association: prostate cancer incidence in the General Practice Research Database with a rate ratio of 1.23 and significantly elevated at 1.40 with more than 36 prescriptions, no effect across ten cancers in Kaiser Permanente, and no effect on lung cancer. These observational results had already prompted randomized trials, including a phase III trial of nearly 3,600 women with early breast cancer.

future_research.gap: Every study identified as biased would have to be redone correctly before the evidence base can be read, and new studies with adequate designs are needed before further trials are launched.
future_research.quote: Moreover, new observational studies using more rigorous designs and analyses that avoid these biases should urgently be undertaken before more randomized trials are initiated in vain.

problems.evidence: Twenty-two studies across different databases and countries reproduced a protective association, and the paper's position is that the agreement carries no evidential weight because the studies share a design defect. Replication is used in the field as a validity argument and this is a worked case where it is not one, with the consequence that expensive trials were launched.
problems.quote: In the case of the association between metformin and cancer, we believe that methodologically inaccurate studies, even if their results are replicated in different settings, should not be the driving force behind long and expensive trials.

problems.evidence: Two studies named immortal time bias and then used an analysis that did not address it, so mentioning the bias functioned as a credential rather than as a correction. Nothing in the publication record distinguishes a study that handled the problem from one that acknowledged it.
problems.quote: Although two of the studies recognized the possibility of immortal time bias, the technique of data analysis required to address it was clearly not appropriate ( 16 , 18 ).

problems.evidence: Three distinct time-structural failures are separated here, misclassified exposure time, unequal exposure opportunity windows, and comparing treatments given at different disease stages, and each is a decision about where a window starts and stops. The exposure window and the comparator's position on the disease course are design parameters with no procedure fixing them, and getting either wrong produces effects up to a 94 percent risk reduction.
problems.quote: Time-related biases include immortal time bias, a bias introduced with time-fixed cohort analyses that misclassify unexposed time as exposed; time-window bias, a bias introduced because of differential exposure opportunity time windows between subjects; and time-lag bias, a bias introduced by comparing treatments given at different stages of the disease ( 1 , 2 ).

problems.evidence: Time-lag bias is a comparator problem rather than a timing problem in the narrow sense: metformin is first-line and the comparators are second- or third-line, so the two groups differ in disease stage by construction of the treatment guidelines. Restricting to comparable stages is an eligibility decision, and the paper reports that studies simply did not make it.
problems.quote: We found that 13 observational studies suffered from immortal time bias; 9 studies had not considered time-window bias, whereas other studies did not consider inherent time-lagging issues when comparing the first-line treatment metformin with second- or third-line treatments.

papers.title: Challenges of guarantee-time bias.
papers.one_line: Applies a naive analysis and three corrections to bisphosphonate use in the BIG 1-98 trial, where the naive hazard ratio of 0.50 becomes 0.99, 0.85 and 0.97 at three landmark times and 0.92 and 0.90 under extended Cox and inverse probability weighting.
papers.what_was_done: Guarantee-time bias arises whenever survival timed from enrollment is compared across groups defined by an event occurring during follow-up, such as tumor response, toxicity onset, seroconversion, or starting a secondary treatment. Three corrections are set out with their properties: conditional landmark analysis, which discards patients and events before the landmark and answers a conditional question; the extended Cox model, which uses all follow-up, keeps full power and allows group membership to change; and inverse probability weighting in two stages, which models the probability of entering the classifying event group in each interval and weights the outcome model by its inverse. In BIG 1-98, 8,010 women were analyzed for disease-free survival by bisphosphonate use. The naive analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.50 with interval 0.43 to 0.60. Landmarks at 12, 24 and 36 months gave 0.99, 0.85 and 0.97, none significant; the extended Cox model gave 0.92 and inverse probability weighting 0.90. The bias was large because roughly 58 percent of bisphosphonate users began therapy at least three years after enrollment. The paper asserts guarantee-time bias should always be suspected when the classifying event occurs during follow-up.

future_research.gap: Weights depend on which predictors enter the first-stage probability model, so the second-stage estimate varies with that choice and can only be probed by sensitivity analysis.
future_research.quote:
We note that because
the weights from the models in the first stage may vary depending on
the predictors used to model the probabilities, the estimates from the
second model stage may also vary.

future_research.gap: Standard statistical software does not implement the two-stage weighting procedure, leaving downloadable macros as the only route.
future_research.quote:
At the present time, the standard statistical software packages do
not provide preprogrammed routines that will develop the two stages.

problems.evidence: Three landmark times on the same data give hazard ratios of 0.99, 0.85 and 0.97 with sample sizes falling from 7,797 to 7,220 as the landmark moves out. The paper presents all three rather than choosing, which is honest reporting and also an admission that no rule selects among them, and it notes the bias depends on how long after enrollment the classifying event tends to occur.
problems.quote:
as we have shown with the BIG 1-98 data,
when the classifying event can occur a long time after the start of
follow-up, or if there are a number of early outcome events, a naive
analysis can be heavily biased in favor of the group with the classifying
event

problems.evidence: The weighting correction replaces a time-related bias with a no-unmeasured-confounders assumption about entry into the classifying event group, which the paper names and then leaves undiagnosed. Its practical advice, to include marginally significant variables that are clinically relevant or improve fit, is a model-building rule and not a check on the assumption.
problems.quote:
An important assumption in this method is that once a patient’s
clinical, disease, and demographic histories are known at a given time,
the decision to move into the classifying event group at that time does
not depend on any other prognostic factors.

problems.evidence: Three corrections are presented with strengths and limitations and no rule for choosing, and they return different numbers on the same data, 0.85 to 0.99 across landmarks against 0.92 and 0.90. The recommendation is to use them as complements, which leaves the reader with a range rather than an estimate.
problems.quote:
IPW is more technically challenging to implement than the conditional landmark approach or the extended Cox model; however, the
method has been used as a complement to the landmark analysis.25

problems.evidence: The weights are used as covariates in the second stage, so the reported hazard ratios are conditional on the probability of group membership, and the paper states there is no packaged implementation. Correct inference after a two-stage weighting procedure is left to downloadable macros whose variance treatment is not described.
problems.quote:
Because the
weights are used as predictors in the second model stage, the HRs are
conditional on the probability of being in the classifying event group.

problems.evidence: The paper gives a concrete positivity check for the first-stage model, that no cell size is zero and no covariate pattern has zero probability of moving into the other group, and flags small data sets as the risk case. It is stated as an implementation caution rather than as a reported diagnostic, and it does not identify which patient histories are unsupported.
problems.quote:
However, it is
important to check that the probability models do not result in cell
sizes of zero or create covariate patterns with zero probability of
moving into the other classifying event group.
